name: Victor Hugo
role: French novelist, peer, republican deputy and senator (1802-1885)
summary: Hugo moved from royalism to a republicanism that joined universal suffrage and free press with lay free schooling, abolition of the death penalty, public relief and a federal United States of Europe. He opposed Louis Bonaparte's coup and lived in exile for nearly twenty years, defended property while wanting it spread to workers, and backed colonisation as a duty of tutelage for 'elder' peoples.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: On 1 March 1871 he told the Assembly that Alsace and Lorraine want to remain French and that Prussia's seizure was fact but not right.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Before the Council of State's theatre commission in 1849 Hugo argued for freedom of the theatre over authority, having had his own plays banned.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Hugo wrote that civilization implies colonisation and colonisation tutelage, granting France a right over Africa and England over Asia, but only as a duty that ends when the ward comes of age.

class-collaboration.rationale: He sought the reconciliation of labour with capital and told the poor to seek change by voting rather than rebelling.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Hugo named the quarrel of right against law as the driving force of progress and judged the June 1848 class insurrection a mistake.

clerical-rule.rationale: He refused to put bishops on public school boards and denounced the Catholic party's bid for control of teaching.

common-currency.rationale: In his Jersey address to the exiles Hugo pictured a single continental currency replacing the varied national coins, as part of the United States of Europe.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: He told the Peace Congress that humanity began in struggle but moves to peace, and that arbitration should replace battles.

conscription.rationale: His pre-1870 programme abolished the 'blood tax' while the 1871 programme he accepted required personal military service for all citizens.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Hugo held that universal suffrage makes the sovereign and in 1871 told the Assembly that 'possession presupposes consent', denying that conquest creates a right.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The programme he accepted in 1871 called for dissolving the Assembly and electing a constituent body to write a republican constitution.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Hugo distinguished elder and younger peoples and spoke of savage nations having a right to civilisation, so he did not hold all civilisations equal.

death-penalty.rationale: In his 15 September 1848 Assembly speech Hugo called the death penalty the special and eternal sign of barbarism and voted for pure, simple and definitive abolition; he kept campaigning for it in exile and after.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: He backed the 1849 proposal to organise public assistance and rejected the view that repression alone suffices against poverty.

decide-locally.rationale: His programme returned to departments, cantons and communes all that falls within their remit, and he looked to an end of centralised administration.

democracy-best.rationale: The day after losing the January 1872 Paris by-election he wrote that universal suffrage may suffer eclipses but is the only mode of government, 'everything by the vote, nothing by the rifle'.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: In his 1872 letter to Léon Richer Hugo called the legal minority of women a slavery that must end, noting there are citizens but no women citizens.

elective-rulers.rationale: Hugo defended universal suffrage as the sovereignty of all and demanded that rulers come from it.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In 1848 he asked to ease the state of siege gradually rather than lift it at once, yet fought its use against the press.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Hugo called for arbitration to replace battles under a sovereign senate of the peoples.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: In 1848 he asked that the inviolability of human life be written into the constitution, as a right above ordinary law.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Hugo wrote that we are brothers by life, equal by birth and death and free by the soul, and demanded equal rights for women and an end to slavery.

equal-outcomes.rationale: He described the equality he wanted as one admitting each person's natural growth, and aimed to ease the climb from labour to property rather than level results.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The contractual mandate he accepted in December 1871 listed a 'truly proportional tax on income', which is a flat-rate tax.

free-trade.rationale: His picture of a federated Europe has no frontiers, customs or octrois and free exchange, and he named customs abolition among the causes he fought for.

gradual-change.rationale: He urged the 'grave and measured step of progress' and peaceful change, yet demanded immediate abolition of the death penalty and called monarchy an usurpation.

job-guarantee.rationale: In 1869 he called the right to work, implied by equality, a superb formula of 1848 and later wanted communal workshops to secure it.

means-match-ends.rationale: He pictured a liberated Europe with 'no act of force against anyone, even to bring about the good' and said progress needs no violent struggle.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Hugo condemned the army's use in the 1851 coup and the passive obedience of its soldiers.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Hugo wrote that the republic is the absolute social principle and so every monarchy is a usurpation, even a legally proclaimed one; he demanded the exclusion of all monarchies in 1871.

more-religion-public.rationale: He wanted the church kept to its own sphere, opposed clerical control of education in 1850 and held that dogma replaces reason.

nation-first.rationale: Hugo told the 1849 Peace Congress that before being French, English or German one is a man, and that nations are homelands while humanity is a family.

national-mission.rationale: Hugo wrote that France is destined to become Europe and create universal hopes for other peoples through her republic.

national-self-determination.rationale: Hugo declared the aim of true politics to be the recognition of all nationalities, and defended Poland, Italy, Crete and Alsace-Lorraine against foreign rule.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Hugo held that the state owes instruction to the child and should organise public assistance, beyond defence and justice.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Hugo held that the state in teaching can only be lay, wanted no bishops on school councils, and in 1872 wrote that instruction must be lay while religious upbringing belongs to the family.

one-party-rule.rationale: Hugo defended a free press, free assembly and pluralism and attacked the single-will rule of 1851.

open-borders.rationale: He called for the effacing of frontiers on the map and for customs and frontiers to vanish in a European federation.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Hugo defended the Assembly's authority against presidential encroachment and rejected monarchy.

party-controls-media.rationale: Hugo fought the state of siege on the press in 1848 and wrote that without liberty of the press there is no valid vote; he demanded absolute freedom of the press and of assembly.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: He wrote that men loaded all rights on their own side and all duties on women's, so that women are slaves in reality though called minors in law.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: In the 1849 Peace Congress and again in 1871 Hugo called for a federation of European peoples, the United States of Europe, under a sovereign senate.

priority-to-poor.rationale: In July 1849 Hugo urged the Assembly to organise public relief and said misery can be destroyed, calling for the worker to be sacred to those who no longer work.

property-fundamental.rationale: Hugo held that property is the result of labour and that striking it would kill labour, though he wanted it made accessible to workers.

rehabilitation.rationale: Hugo's own list of the causes he fought for includes penalties decreasing as education grows, and he later said socialism means penalty absorbed by education.

religion-illusion.rationale: Hugo attacked dogma and the Catholic clergy while affirming God and the soul, so his own words point both ways on religion as consoling illusion.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Hugo took up arms against the 1851 coup as 'my right as a citizen and my duty as a representative', invoking Article 68 which deposed a president who broke the constitution.

restore-past-order.rationale: Hugo said the past cannot stand in front of the future and that reaction must give way to progress, in the 1872 address to Paris.

return-lost-territory.rationale: He said Alsace and Lorraine would remain French and that France would take them back, though through republic and federation rather than war.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Hugo held that all monarchy is usurpation and called the Second Empire a crime, rejecting any sacral kingship.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: He urged in 1849 that the Louvre be completed as a metropolis of the mind and denounced the pillage of the Summer Palace.

separate-church-state.rationale: In the January 1850 education debate Hugo said he would keep and deepen the old separation of church and state, 'the church at home and the state at home'.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Hugo held that Article 68 required the deposing of a president who broke the constitution and spent his life opposing a ruler who did.

state-harmful.rationale: He asked the state to provide schooling and relief and wrote that the republic is the sovereignty of the person over himself, not the absence of state.

strong-leader.rationale: Napoleon the Little and the History of a Crime denounce rule by one man who overrides the Assembly, and Hugo spent nearly twenty years in exile rather than accept it.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: He wanted a lay state keeping an eye on seminaries and teaching congregations and listed the nation's recovery of church monuments among his causes.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He called for customs barriers to be abolished and praised Cobden for creating free trade.

taxation-theft.rationale: Hugo's programme called for a truly proportional tax on income and an end to the blood tax, treating taxation as legitimate in principle.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Hugo called conquest 'rapine, nothing more' and condemned the Anglo-French plunder of the Summer Palace as banditry.

total-state.rationale: Hugo ranked liberty above forms of government and rejected authority over theatre, press and conscience, including in education where he wanted freedom to teach under lay supervision.

universal-morality.rationale: The preface to Actes et Paroles says right is divine and absolute while law is earthly and relative, with conscience as its voice.

war-builds-character.rationale: Hugo told the Peace Congress that the law of God is peace not war and that killing will cease to be glory, calling war a barbaric expense.

widespread-small-property.rationale: He stated that access to property should be made easy for the working man, and later spoke of property democratised and accessible to all.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Hugo wrote that duty is the law of his life and that the good citizen stands at the disposal of duty, in office or out.

notes: Read from his own collected speeches and pamphlets (Actes et Paroles I-III, Napoleon the Little, History of a Crime). His early royalism and Catholicism (before about 1848) are not used: answers reflect the mature republican position held from the 1848 Assembly to his death; the later speeches of 1876-1885 and the 1879 banquet addresses were not read. Novels and poems were not used as evidence of his positions. Themes searched: economy (property, tax, work, trade, relief), government (suffrage, executive, army, press, courts, local government), society (church and school, women, family, colonisation), world (war, Europe, nationalities, intervention, annexation), liberty (death penalty, press, theatre). Nothing found on healthcare, drugs, abortion, guns, immigration levels, environment or technology.
